# Life insurance term vs whole

Reviewed May 2024 after the Nationwide remortgage. Started because a financial adviser at a client's networking breakfast (Gareth Pryce, Pryce Wealth, Harrogate) told me I "needed" whole of life. I was suspicious, so I did the sums.

## What we already had

- **My policy**: Legal & General level term, £250,000, 25 years from March 2017 to March 2042. £21.40 a month. Policy LG-TRM-7720418
- **Javier's**: Vitality level term, £150,000, to 2045, £17.50 a month. Started 2020
- Death in service: none, both self-employed or small employer
- Both written in trust (L&G form done 2017, Vitality's online trust 2021). Trustees: each other plus my sister Claire

## What "enough" means

If I'm not here, what does Javier need, and until when? Worked out on 18 May 2024:

1. Clear the Meanwood mortgage: £191,880
2. Replace my contribution to household spending until Theo is 21 (2039): about £1,400 a month for 15 years. Lump sum equivalent at a cautious 3% real return: roughly £203,000
3. Childcare cover he'd suddenly need: £6,000 a year for 6 years = £36,000
4. Funeral and admin: £8,000
5. Minus what's already there: pensions (death benefits go to nominated beneficiaries, ~£120,000), ISA £38,000, the Cardigan Road flat (could be sold, net maybe £80,000 after the BTL loan)

Gap: about £200,000 more than existing assets. So £250,000 on me is roughly right, maybe slightly short as the kids' costs rise.

## Term

Pays only if death happens within the term. Nothing back at the end if I'm still around (which is the hope). That's what makes it cheap.

- Level term: the sum assured stays fixed. Mine
- Decreasing term: sum drops roughly in line with a repayment mortgage. Cheaper. Fine if the only purpose is the mortgage
- Inflation-linked: rises with RPI, premium rises too

Quotes for an extra £100,000 level term to 2039 on me (non-smoker, 41, BMI 24, thyroid declared): Aviva £8.90/month, L&G £9.65, Zurich £10.10.

## Whole of life

Pays whenever death happens, so it always pays. Premiums are far higher because the insurer is certain to pay eventually.

Gareth's quote: Royal London whole of life, £100,000 sum, guaranteed premiums, **£84.20 a month**. Over 40 years that's £40,416 paid in for a £100,000 sum. If invested at 5% instead, the same £84.20 a month would grow to roughly £128,000.

Where whole of life does make sense:

- Inheritance tax planning, to fund an IHT bill on an estate over the nil rate bands (£325,000 + £175,000 residence band each). We are nowhere near £1m combined
- Someone with a dependant who'll need support forever, e.g. a disabled adult child
- People who can't make themselves invest the difference

None of those apply. Gareth's commission would have been around 100% of the first year's premiums, which might explain the enthusiasm.

## Critical illness

The adviser also pushed CI. Actually a more useful question for a freelancer: if I'm ill and can't work, there's no sick pay. Decided on **income protection** instead: Cirencester Friendly, 4-week deferred period, £1,800 a month benefit, to age 60, £36.10 a month. Started July 2024, policy CF-IP-50178.

## Decision

- Keep both existing term policies
- Add £100,000 decreasing term with Aviva to 2039 (£7.20 a month, policy AV-LIF-61205), started 1 June 2024
- No whole of life
- Income protection as above

Monthly total for all of it: £82.20, which is less than the one whole of life policy on its own. Updated in [[Budget spreadsheet]] (life cover line) and [[Presupuesto familiar]].
